title: Ajahn Funn: If the mind still has existence (bhava), that means it is not yet free from suffering. When the mind has no existence, it…
content:
Ehipassiko: Come and See Physical and Mental Phenomena Within Yourself

If the mind still has existence (bhava), that means it is not yet free from suffering. When the mind has no existence, it is finished with existence because it does not grasp anything, does not cling to anything. It is merely the knower. Where would it get existence from? Having heard this, you must reverse the current, turn inward. Ehipassiko – inviting all beings to come and see the Dhamma. See your own physical phenomena (rūpa dhamma) and mental phenomena (nāma dhamma). Physical phenomena are this individual body of ours. Mental phenomena are this mind of ours. Let us come and see. Is this Dhamma wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), or indeterminate (abyākata)? We must know. Wholesome Dhamma is happiness. Unwholesome Dhamma is suffering. Indeterminate Dhamma – neither happiness nor suffering, neither good nor evil, negating all.

Therefore, when we all want freedom from suffering, we must know that freedom occurs when the mind is peaceful. When our mind is peaceful, then freedom is right there. No need to seek elsewhere. This is the practice.

title: Ajahn Funn: When it’s light, it sees. When it’s heavy, it sees. When it’s dark, it knows that. When it’s bright, it knows that. Don’t…
content:
The Knower Does Not Become Extinct, Does Not Cease

When it’s light, it sees. When it’s heavy, it sees. When it’s dark, it knows that. When it’s bright, it knows that. Don’t go grasping anything. If it’s dark, don’t grasp the darkness. Just take the knowing itself. Take the Knower, knowing that it’s dark. If it’s neutral, observe neutrality. The Knower that is neutral exists. When it’s gone, the Knower that knows it’s gone exists. The Knower exists like that. It does not become extinct, does not cease, does not become nothing. That is why it is called the Knower. Buddho is the Knower. It exists like that. It does not cease, does not become nothing. It has existed from the very beginning. Pubbe te dhammā — phenomena exist like that, but no individual had known them. We must know them for ourselves. The Dhamma exists like that. Before the Buddha’s enlightenment, it existed like that. After enlightenment, it existed like that. But we hadn’t encountered it; we hadn’t yet discovered it. That’s how it is.

Therefore, make the discovery now. Sit in meditation, direct your mind inward, contemplate that knowing itself. Knowing has no self, no being. It is just knowing there, just that one thing — knowing. The Knower is not subject to death, not subject to breaking or destruction, not subject to hunger or poverty, not subject to suffering or hardship, not subject to trouble or annoyance.

title: Ajahn Funn: Within us, everything is complete. The 84,000 Dhamma aggregates, having listened, are not anything far away. When gathered in, they are: the Suttas…
content:
The Mūla-Kammaṭṭhāna: Hair, Body Hair, Nails, Teeth, Skin – Not a Person

Within us, everything is complete. The 84,000 Dhamma aggregates, having listened, are not anything far away. When gathered in, they are: the Suttas – the inhalation of breath; the Vinaya – the exhalation of breath; the Paramattha – the knowing one inside.

The Paramattha is arranged into seven books – the Abhidhamma seven books. When we first hear this, it seems far away, but when explained, it is right within ourselves. Kāmāvacara kusala cittaṃ – the mind that thinks, that constructs, that concocts – where is it? Everything arises from this mind. Wholesome and unwholesome arise from the mind, not from anywhere else. Somanassa – happiness; when our mind delights in wholesome things, it becomes wholesome; when it delights in unwholesome things, it becomes unwholesome. Ñāṇa – knowledge; knowledge is not elsewhere; our mind is the knower. Whatever form we take as an object – beautiful form or ugly form – if we take any form as object, we create a state of being there, establish a state of being there.

When we have heard and listened, ehipassiko – the Dhamma invites us to come and see. He taught to come and see Dhamma, not to go and see Dhamma elsewhere. He taught to come and see our own rūpa-dhamma (material phenomena) and nāma-dhamma (mental phenomena). The material phenomena of our own body – what is there? We assume we are a person, a woman, a man – where is that exactly? We should look closely.

title: Ajahn Funn: Whether good or evil, tassa dāyādā bhavissanti — I will be the heir of that kamma. Whatever kamma we have done, whether merit…
content:
Old Kamma Not Finished, New Kamma Adding – Stop It by Sitting in Samādhi

Whether good or evil, tassa dāyādā bhavissanti — I will be the heir of that kamma. Whatever kamma we have done, whether merit or demerit, we will receive its result accordingly. Kalyāṇaṃ — good kamma. How can we know it? In short: our mind is good, has happiness and ease, light in body and self. That is what good kamma is like, isn't it? Pāpakaṃ — bad kamma. What is it like? The mind is not good — miserable, troubled, agitated, not calm. It goes creating kamma, enmity, danger — heavy, sluggish, drowsy, dull, miserable, hardship — that is bad kamma. Mental kamma (mano-kamma), the mind's inclining. Whatever kamma we incline toward, let go of it. Do not think about it. All kamma — we think it into being. If we do not think it, it does not arise. Old kamma is not yet finished, and we keep adding new kamma. Will it ever end? If you want kamma to end, stop it. Do not create kamma. Even sitting here, you still create it. Bhave bhavā sambhavanti — it creates little and great states of becoming right here. When we see it, cut it off. That is vipassanā. Cut off evil, cut off all mental objects.

title: Ajahn Funn: We have been born and have only looked at external work, only studied other things. We have never studied our own conditioned body…
content:
Diseases Everywhere in the Body – Contemplate to Make Them Disappear

We have been born and have only looked at external work, only studied other things. We have never studied our own conditioned body (saṅkhāra) even once. So now let us study it. Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin – how can they be 'me' or 'mine'? Contemplate and investigate like this. Our conditioned body is now plagued by this illness and that illness – nothing but diseases.

The Buddha taught: cakkhurogo – disease of the eye; sotarogo – disease of the ear; ghānarogo – disease of the nose; jivhārogo – disease of the tongue; kāyārogo – disease of the body; manorogo – disease of the mind-heart; pādarogo – disease of the feet; kesārogo – disease of the hair; nakharogo – disease of the nails; dantārogo – disease of the teeth; tacorogo – disease of the skin; maṁsarogo – disease of the flesh; nahārurogo – disease of the sinews; aṭṭhirogo – disease of the bones. That's how diseases arise. Therefore, the Buddha taught us to contemplate these things, to investigate them. When our mind is calm, these diseases disappear. If the mind is not calm, they become disease and danger. That's how it is.

title: Ajahn Funn: We depend on the teachings of the Buddha. To begin with, we’ve done a candle-circumambulation and made an offering to the Triple Gem.…
content:
The Triple Gem Are Like Gems: The Buddha’s Heart Was Clear Like a Gem

We depend on the teachings of the Buddha. To begin with, we’ve done a candle-circumambulation and made an offering to the Triple Gem. “Triple” means three. Which three? The gem of the Buddha, the gem of the Dhamma, the gem of the Saṅgha: These gems are our refuge.

Now, the Buddha isn’t a gem. The Dhamma isn’t a gem. The Saṅgha isn’t a gem. They’re like gems. Gems are bright and clear, like a clear mirror. The Buddha’s heart was clear like a gem. That’s how he was able to know all levels of pleasure and pain. Heavens and hells, he saw them all—all levels of goodness and evil. That’s why he was able to set out the religion for all of us, lay and ordained.

Those of us born in these latter days haven’t had the opportunity to see the Lord Buddha. We’ve met only with the Dhamma, the teachings he taught. What he taught wasn’t anywhere else far away. In the list of the virtues of the Dhamma, it says that the Dhamma is ehipassiko: It’s for calling all living beings to come and see. It’s not for calling them to go and see. He wants us to come and see the Dhamma. And so where do we come to see the Dhamma? Right here at our rūpa-dhamma, or physical phenomena, and our nāma-dhamma, or mental phenomena.

title: Ajahn Funn: Let the body be at ease. After all, you want ease. Make your mind empty. Make it still. Whatever it’s stuck on, whatever…
content:
Have Compassion for Yourself: Look at Your Own Heart

Let the body be at ease. After all, you want ease. Make your mind empty. Make it still. Whatever it’s stuck on, whatever it’s snared by, disentangle it right now. When you die, you can’t disentangle things. When the time comes, you can’t disentangle things. But right now you can. When the harm of your actions comes to you, you can’t stop it. So counteract it now from the start. When the time comes, you’ll go running to this or that venerable old monk to show you some compassion. Whoever’s in trouble will go running to them, to ask for compassion. The problem is that you don’t show any compassion for yourself.

So have some compassion for yourself. Look at yourself. When you’re sitting in meditation like this, you can’t get devas, Indras, or Brahmās to do your looking for you. So sit and look at yourself. Are you happy or miserable? Good or bad? Try to see for yourself. It’s not that the weather’s good or the weather’s bad. Look. When there’s suffering, it’s not that the weather’s suffering. It’s your heart. So look.

title: Ajahn Funn: They teach us to meditate to know a calm mind — whether the mind is good or not. When it is calm, it…
content:
Vipassanā: Knowing the Origin and Cessation of Saṅkhāra

They teach us to meditate to know a calm mind — whether the mind is good or not. When it is calm, it becomes clear, giving rise to vipassanā-ñāṇa (insight knowledge). What does it know? It knows the origin of saṅkhāra, knows the cessation of saṅkhāra — that is vipassanā. It knows the origin and cessation of saṅkhāra, knows the suffering and the danger in saṅkhāra. When it sees the suffering, the danger, the peril of saṅkhāra, it cuts off. It does not want suffering, does not want danger. See? Where does it come from? It knows the origin but not the cessation. Where do all these saṅkhāras come from? They come from our own mind — the concocting, the fabricating, the thinking, the intending. Where does the intending come from? Now, having heard and listened: ehipassiko — "come and see." Call all beings to come see the Dhamma. Where to see the Dhamma? See our own rūpa-dhamma (material phenomena) and nāma-dhamma (mental phenomena). Rūpa-dhamma is our own physical body. Come see: two arms, two legs, one head.

title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore, let us all strive to practice meditation, to focus and look, to determine and observe. You don't need to find something elsewhere…
content:
Observing What Is Yours: Everything Is Already Within Yourself

Therefore, let us all strive to practice meditation, to focus and look, to determine and observe. You don't need to find something elsewhere to observe. Observe what is yours. You already have everything within yourself. Emptiness is already there. Non-emptiness is already there. Happiness is already there. Suffering is already there. Everything is here right now. Observe what you have. However it is established, keep watching it just like that. Watch to know. And do not grasp this or that as a self, as a soul. The matter is simply that. We must all understand this point. That is why we come to do kammaṭṭhāna – kamma means action, what we do; ṭhāna means foundation, place. Establish it to abide. If it is empty, know it. If it is not empty, know it. To abandon, we must contemplate the basic kammaṭṭhāna. The teacher taught the basic kammaṭṭhāna so that we would know according to reality. He taught about hair so that we would know what hair is like. Is it a person? Is it something? Is this hair clean or unclean? This is the method to remove our lust, greed, hatred, and delusion, to remove our craving concerning self-identity.

title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore He said: suffering (dukkha) should be comprehended, should be contemplated, leading to its origin (samudaya). We all know about samudaya – beings…
content:
Tracing Dependent Origination Back to Ignorance (Avijjā)

Therefore He said: suffering (dukkha) should be comprehended, should be contemplated, leading to its origin (samudaya). We all know about samudaya – beings are sunk in the great ocean, as prey for fish. That is the case. Pāpo pāpaṃ – sunk in the great ocean, meaning deluded by conventions (sammuti). The Buddha investigated: where does suffering come from? He traced it back upstream. At first He contemplated: where does suffering come from? What are its causes and conditions? It comes from illness, disease, affliction. Where do those come from? They come from aging, decrepitude, deterioration. Where does that come from? From birth. Where does birth come from? From becoming (bhava) – that is, taking a state of being. Where does that becoming come from? He contemplated: it comes from clinging (upādāna). Wherever we cling, we take becoming there. Look: our becoming, small and large – becoming comes from clinging. Where does clinging come from? From craving (taṇhā). Where does craving come from? From feeling (vedanā) – painful feeling, pleasant feeling. Where do these feelings come from? From contact (phassa). Where does contact come from? From the sense bases (āyatana) – eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind. Where do these sense bases come from? From mind-and-body (nāmarūpa). Where does nāmarūpa come from? From consciousness (viññāṇa) – rebirth-linking consciousness. Where does consciousness come from? From saṅkhārā, fabrications. Where do saṅkhārā come from? From ignorance (avijjā).
